title: The monkey and the pitch
hook: a monkey caught in a hunter's sticky pitch by grabbing with every limb (SN 47.7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: gocara, the quail's plowed field. Your own ground is the four foundations of mindfulness.

In the Buddha's story, hunters in the Himalaya have a trick for catching monkeys. No net. No arrow. Just a smear of sticky pitch along the trails where monkeys travel. A wise monkey sees it and keeps going. A curious one touches it with one paw. Stuck. So it uses the other paw to pull the first one free. Stuck. Then a foot. Then the other foot. Then, out of ideas, it tries its mouth.
screen: `PITCH ON THE MONKEY TRAIL.` → `ONE PAW. THEN THE OTHER.` → `THEN THE FEET. THEN THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: This is SN 47.7, right next to the quail. The Buddha describes three kinds of mountain country: rugged places where neither monkeys nor people go, places where monkeys go but people don't, and even, pleasant places where both go. In that third kind, hunters lay pitch along the trails. The foolish monkey, stuck at five points, lies there crying out, and the hunter does with it as he pleases. The lesson matches the quail's: keep to your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness. The range of others is the five cords of sense pleasure. But this picture adds something. The quail story is about where you are. The monkey story is about how you get stuck: by trying to get unstuck the same way you got stuck. Every limb that grabs to free the first gets caught too. An argument you try to win with one more message. A craving you try to settle with one more taste. A worry you try to think your way out of. The pitch is laid where life is pleasant; that's the point of putting it there. Mindfulness is the pause before the second paw: seeing the pitch as pitch. The text doesn't call the monkey wicked or the forest evil. The wise monkey sees the pitch and walks around it. That closes six days on right mindfulness: remembering to notice, the gatekeeper, the bowl of oil, the six animals and their post, the quail's own ground, and the monkey.
screen: `THREE KINDS OF MOUNTAIN COUNTRY.` · `STUCK AT FIVE POINTS.` · `GRABBING TO GET FREE STICKS YOU TOO.` · `SEE THE PITCH AS PITCH.` · then, large: `DON'T GRAB THE PITCH.`

segments.voice: Look for one sticky place, a thought you keep returning to, a sound you keep resisting, and notice the second paw: the urge to fix it or push it away right now. Let your hands rest open on your knees and just watch the pull; it may stay, and you're only learning where the pitch is.
Makkata, monkey. The trap that holds you tighter the more you grab to get free.
Your line: don't grab the pitch. Grabbing to get free only sticks you tighter. Day three hundred ninety-four, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use this simile to describe how grasping compounds itself; many practitioners work with it by pausing to notice an urge before acting on it, in meditation and in daily life.

match.prompt: match the pieces of the story.

myth: the monkey is caught in a hunter's net
it's sticky pitch smeared along the trails.
each limb the monkey uses to free itself gets stuck too
two paws, two feet, and finally its mouth.
the sutta calls sense pleasures evil
it calls them the range of others, where the hunter can catch you; the wise monkey simply walks around.

fork.setup: you're a monkey. one paw is stuck in the hunter's pitch. what does the foolish monkey in the story do next?
options: grabs with the other paw to pull it free
fork.reveal: it grabs with the other paw, and that sticks too; then the feet, then the mouth. the way out it tries is the way in.

original.note: Pali makkaṭa: monkey, the animal that gives this sutta its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning to avoid temptation.
what it means: the trap tightens when you grab to get free; mindfulness sees the pitch before the second grab.
what a scholar hears: the sutta names three kinds of mountain country, where neither monkeys nor people go, where only monkeys go, and where both go; the pitch is laid in the third.
guess: a monkey, caught by grabbing to get free
a hunter who sets traps on mountain trails
a sticky resin smeared on forest paths

chat.says: Why do I get more stuck the harder I try to get unstuck?
options: Like the monkey in the pitch: each grab to get free sticks another paw.
You just haven't grabbed hard enough yet; one more push will do it.
Because pleasant things are evil, and you should never go near them.
chat.meaning: In SN 47.7 the monkey frees one paw with another and ends up stuck at five points. Mindfulness is the pause before the second grab.

Himalaya.meaning: the great mountain range where the story is set

pitch.meaning: a sticky, tar-like resin hunters smeared on trails
